x: This reference describes the inner workings of Middle-earth: Shadow of War. It covers the layout of the executable, the engine objects that run the game, how the game streams and stores data, the world format, scripting, rendering, effects, audio, animation and physics; the gameplay systems built on top of them (AI, combat, items, the Nemesis system, quests, user interface and saves); and how the three PC builds of the game (Steam, GOG and the Microsoft Store) differ. The engine is Monolith Productions' in-house engine; the build paths left in the executable name the project Kraken ( proj\Kraken\code\... ). It builds on Havok 2016.2.0-r1 ( hk2016 2 0 r1 ) for physics, AI navigation, cloth and scripting (HavokScript), Wwise for audio, Bink 2 for video and Scaleform GFx 4.5 for the user interface.

Every address here belongs to the Steam release, game version 1.21 ( ShadowOfWar.exe , 117,732,784 bytes, linked in August 2018). The same version also ships as the GOG release and as the Microsoft Store package: the same engine source, data formats and object layouts, with every function and global at another address. Game builds compares the three, gives the addresses of key engine objects in each and describes where each build keeps its saves.

- Static analysis of the executable: a full instruction decode of every function, cross references, vtables and run-time type information, string references, the exception-unwind tables and the C runtime's initializer tables. - Inspection of the running game: reading live objects, containers and engine state, with a control for every census (a known-good object or a deliberately wrong value checked in the same pass), and comparing values decoded from the shipped files with the values the engine holds. - Parsing the shipped archives: every container format and data format the game reads, decoded until every byte of a format is accounted for and the decode matches what the running game loaded. - Thread sampling: suspending one thread at a time, unwinding its stack with the executable's own unwind data, and aggregating thousands of samples into call trees and per-frame order. - Emulation: running individual engine functions in an emulator against a snapshot of live memory, to see exactly what they read and decide. Numbers such as "950 of 950" are the measurements a statement rests on: how many cases were checked and how many agreed.

- The executable has no relocation table, so it always loads at 0x140000000 . Code and static data addresses are given as offsets from that base (RVAs): 0x1A864C is the address 0x140000000 + 0x1A864C = 0x1401A864C. The GOG and Microsoft Store executables are relocatable and lay their code out differently, so a Steam RVA does not apply to them (see Game builds). - [base+0x26FFAA8] means "the pointer stored at RVA 0x26FFAA8". [GM+0x6C68] means "the pointer stored 0x6C68 bytes into the object GM". - Heap addresses change every run and are never given. - vt 0x1F68920 names a class by its vtable's RVA when the class has no recoverable name; vf10 is the vtable's eleventh slot (counting from 0). - GameDB records and categories are written in backticks with their category path, for example Character/Models .
Each chapter ends with the questions that are still open, phrased with what would settle them.

t: Game builds: Steam, GOG and Microsoft Store
x: Shadow of War 1.21 ships on PC as three builds: the Steam release, the GOG release (the game with its Expansion Pass) and the Microsoft Store package played through the Xbox app. They run the same engine on the same data formats and the same object layouts. They differ in where every function and global sits in the executable, in packaging, and in the platform layer that supplies accounts and save storage. Every address elsewhere in this reference belongs to the Steam build; this chapter describes the other two and how an address carries over.

The Steam image has no relocation table (file characteristics 0x23, IMAGE FILE RELOCS STRIPPED ; DLL characteristics 0x8120, no DYNAMIC BASE ), so it always loads at 0x140000000 and an address is the same in every run. It carries an Authenticode certificate table (0xCE0 bytes) and a PE checksum. Its 17 section names do not describe their contents (see The executable). It exports 286 names: the Wwise sound engine's API, Scaleform's system and matrix functions, two memory pool ids and an assert hook.

The GOG image is a later build of the same engine source (see How the builds correspond): - Relocatable. File characteristics 0x22 (relocations kept), DLL characteristics 0x8160 ( DYNAMIC BASE , HIGH ENTROPY VA , NX COMPAT , TERMINAL SERVER AWARE ) and a relocation table of 0x72EDC bytes: Windows picks the base at every start, and an address is the module base plus the GOG build's own RVA. - Identified by size and time stamp. The file is unsigned and its PE checksum is 0; its size (44,474,880 bytes), time stamp (0x631BB422) and image size (0x2E3D000) identify it. - Runtime libraries. It imports the Visual C++ 2015-2022 runtime ( MSVCP140 , VCRUNTIME140 , the universal C runtime, mfc140u ) and delay-loads d3d11.dll and amd ags x64.dll . - Steamworks without Steam. It still imports four Steamworks functions, SteamInternal ContextInit , SteamInternal CreateInterface , SteamAPI GetHSteamPipe and SteamAPI GetHSteamUser , so steam api64.dll ships beside it. It does not import SteamAPI Init , which the Steam build calls first in its initialization (0x11798AC). - Exports. Steam's 286 names plus GetModuleVersion . Its section table is an ordinary one, and its names say what each section holds: Section RVA range Access Contents Steam build --- --- --- --- --- .text 0x0001000 - 0x1DA0F36 read, execute the engine's code .interpr 0x1DA1000 - 0x1DAA364 read, execute HavokScript's interpreter .sdata 0x1D88000 - 0x1D91400: its three functions pair with GOG's at one shift of +0x19000, the first (0x1D88000, 13,176 bytes) the one that raises the script VM's run-time errors ("attempt to index a nil value") .rdata 0x1DAB000 - 0x25AEE96 read vtables, strings, constant tables .xtext .data 0x25AF000 - 0x2AC5F58 read, write the writable globals .idata .pdata 0x2AC6000 - 0x2CA2B2C read 162,713 unwind entries .pdata , 163,575 entries .gfids , .tls , RDATA 0x2CA3000 - 0x2CA5020 read ( .tls read, write) small tables .SHARED 0x2CA6000, 8 bytes read, write, shared marked IMAGE SCN MEM SHARED : one copy for every process that runs the image .rsrc 0x2CA7000 - 0x2DC9F70 read resources .reloc 0x2DCA000 - 0x2E3CEDC read relocations none The last column holds because paired addresses land in the matching sections: Steam's vtables and the hash table at 0x1DB50D0 (in .xtext ) pair with addresses in GOG's .rdata , and Steam's global slots (in .idata ) with addresses in GOG's .data .

All three hold the archives, the Game\ folder and the executable's folder. GOG adds its own files: goggame-1324471032.info describes the game (product 1324471032) and goggame-1911721374.info the Expansion Pass (product 1911721374, root product 1324471032); the game's play task runs x64\ShadowOfWar.exe with x64 as its working folder. The Store package adds the package files ( AppxManifest.xml , AppxBlockMap.xml , AppxSignature.p7x , resources.pri , Localization\ , SplashScreen.png ) and xboxservices.config . The Game\ folder holds the same five entries in every build: SKU.cfg , projectconsole.cfg , cinematics , interface and sound . SKU.cfg and projectconsole.cfg are byte-identical on Steam and GOG.

- GOG ships 71 archives: Steam's 76 without the five high-resolution texture archives ( uhdmip , uhdmip DLC1 - uhdmip DLC4 , 17.3 GB together). The other 71 have the same sizes as Steam's, and those compared byte for byte ( Patch DLC3 , 3,437,374,050 bytes, and the config list) are identical. - The Store ships 66: Steam's without those five, Blade , Lithlad , Patch 04 , Patch 04 LC and Presentations ptbr (the package declares no Brazilian Portuguese). Of the 66, 37 have Steam's sizes. The other 29 ( Patch 03 and Patch 05 - Patch 13 , Patch DLC1 - Patch DLC5 , each with its LC twin except Patch 12 LC ) carry the updates in another split: Steam's Patch 09 is 5,545,787,101 bytes and the Store's 546,573,005; Steam's Patch 12 is an empty archive and the Store's holds 311,972,138 bytes, while the Store's Patch 08 is the empty one. - The config list is written for both layouts: each high-resolution archive is listed twice, as ..\uhdmip.Arch06 and as uhdmip.Arch06 , under the list's own comment "'../' needed for steam, flat needed for UWP". Steam and GOG keep it beside the executable in x64\ , the Store in UWP64\ . How the list is read and searched is in Archives and file formats. - Texture tiers. Without the uhdmip archives, GOG and the Store lack the 8,752 .texuhd files (the highest texture tier) those archives hold, of 10,297 in the Steam build; a texture whose .texuhd shipped there is drawn at most from its .tex0 (see Archives and file formats).

GOG is the same code at other addresses. Of 839 functions compared instruction by instruction with addresses and branch targets masked, 833 have the same instructions as their Steam counterparts; the other six were confirmed by reading them or by the order in which they register with the engine. An alignment of the two images by function bytes, propagated through call sites and vtables, pairs about 160,000 functions and 76,000 data addresses. The compiler's inlining differs in places: the quest-slot check 0x596FF0 is folded into its only caller, and the identity-scale look rebuild 0x1BC3AA8 has no standalone copy, only its callees. The Store build is a separate compile of the same source for the Universal Windows Platform, linked ten minutes after Steam's. Stack frames differ (the dead-body cull's locals at [rsp+0x20] and [rbp+0x67] on Steam sit at [rsp+0x30] and [rsp+0x38] on the Store), so many bodies do not match byte for byte. The same alignment pairs about 84,000 functions and 26,000 data addresses; the rest is matched by structure: strings, call-graph position, constants and the field offsets a function uses. Registration tables pair exactly. Tables the engine fills at start-up keep their order and ids. The 110 attack-predicate registrations have the same kinds and flags in the same order on Steam and GOG, and the 40 animation codec evaluators of the three codec registration tables pair one to one on GOG and the Store, by the FourCC each registration carries as an immediate (see Animation).

Object layouts agree wherever they were compared. Read in running games with the Steam build's field offsets, the captain records ( FactionMember ) and characters read correctly on 542 of 542 captains in 9 of 9 pools and 17 of 17 spawned characters on GOG, and on 543 of 543 captains and 65 of 65 spawned characters on the Store. State that does not depend on where the player stands agrees too: - Static world objects. Objects placed by the region's data have the same count per class in the same place. On the same save in the same region, all eight AI-node classes have equal counts on GOG and the Store, among them 153 ranged-attack nodes, 1,292 route nodes, 5,443 menace places, 753 flee nodes and 114 gather nodes. - GameDB category databases are allocated at start-up in a fixed order, so the distance between two of their heap pointers is the same in every build: 0xE18 between the databases in [base+0x2701708] and [base+0x2701D10] on Steam, GOG and the Store. Some pools allocated at start-up are larger on the Store: the inventory item's second base class (vt 0x1FDABD0 on Steam) has 10,223 objects on Steam and GOG and 14,809 on the Store, with the constructors confirming the class.

Globals keep their order within a run of one object file's data, so neighbors keep their distances: the client shell's slot is 0x10 below the GameManager's and the main scene's 0x08 above it in all three builds. Across the image the shift changes from run to run, and no single offset converts addresses. One block of flags is laid out differently: the engine switch bytes 0x2A34D67, 0x2A34D6B, 0x2A34D6C, 0x2A34D72 and 0x2A34D8E are packed into one block on Steam and on the Store (one shift, +0x66AA9B, confirmed by code for three of the five) but are five separate 8-byte-aligned globals on GOG, each with its own shift.

When bytes do not settle a pair, these readers do, each independent of the others: - A data cell by the code that addresses it. Steam's RIP-relative instructions for a cell, with displacements and branch targets masked, occur once in the other image; the cell that instruction addresses is the twin. On GOG this confirmed 286 of 327 data pairs with no conflict. - A vtable by its slots , when its methods are already paired, and by live object counts for classes whose objects come from region data (above). Slot shapes alone cannot tell apart subclasses that share a base class's slots. - A class through its descriptor: the class-name string, the create function that references it, the constructor it calls, and the vtable that constructor stores at [this] . - A factory by its allocation size , and a function by the one caller both images share. - An import thunk is never a function's twin. Where Steam calls an initializer, the Store build calls memset at the same position (the initializer itself, Steam's 0x596E84, exists in the Store build instruction for instruction at 0x34644D0), so a pairing by call position alone names the memset import thunk.

SteamAPI Init is the first call of the game's initialization 0x11798AC, and the storage interface comes from the SteamClient017 interface's slot 17 (0x1179068). The save reader 0x119A2C8 reads through Steam's remote storage when the platform object's cloud check (its slot 221) passes: it asks ISteamRemoteStorage::GetFileSize (slot 15, through 0x11A6FB8), allocates that many bytes and calls FileRead for exactly that count (slot 1, through 0x11A6FEC); only a read that returns a different count falls back to the local file. It then decrypts as many bytes as the file's own header names, whatever the read returned. Saves are written with FileWrite (slot 0, through 0x52C348).

The GOG build has no store account: it names its save after the computer (the executable imports GetComputerNameW ) and keys it with the account value 0, where the Steam build uses the Steam account number.

Addresses and offsets in this section are the Store build's own. - The app container. The game process runs with an app-container token at low integrity, inside a job object. It can read its own package and the package's per-user data folders, among them %LOCALAPPDATA%\Packages\WarnerBros.Interactive.WB-Kraken ktmk1xygcecda\LocalState . Other folders of the Windows profile, such as Downloads, deny it access. It may start child processes. - Xbox Live. The Store build signs the player in through the Xbox Live services library. The local profile is reached from the client shell's user list ( +0xEB8 , current index +0xED0 ) and has the Store vtable 0x2C411C0. It holds the sign-in wrapper at +0x168 , whose [+0x30] is the services library's user; that user's implementation, at [+0x10] , holds the Xbox user id ( +0x18 ), the gamertag ( +0x38 ) and the web account id ( +0x98 ) as wide strings. - The storage request. After the sign-in completes, the profile asks for save storage through 0xF60720 (also reached from its vtable slot 2). Before the request proper, at 0xF60B15, it calls StoreConfiguration.IsStoreWebAccountId with the web account id and never uses the result. When that call throws (inside the game it fails with E POINTER , and every measured start ended this way), the catch handlers at 0xF60E9C and 0xF60EC9 mark the request finished before the code that copies the Xbox user id (0xF60B27) and the storage request itself (0xF60B6D) have run, and nothing asks again. The profile then has no storage provider: the game neither loads a save nor keeps one in that run. The profile's request state, Store offsets: Offset Meaning --- --- +0x18F failed (the gate of vtable slot 2) +0x198 done; while it is set the profile save 0x60FF90 is refused by its gate 0x60FEE4 +0x19B in flight +0x1A0 the prompt shown (-1 for none) +0x1A8 the Xbox user id, parsed from the services library's text +0x1C0 the storage provider (set by 0xDF1ED0, which adds a reference to the new one and releases the old) Storage handed to the profile after the request has failed is not taken as a save to load: the game is by then set up for a run without one, and its next save writes an empty profile into that storage.

The three builds write the same format: a SOM3 container around a SAVE version 2 file holding the profile sections and the three slots (see Saves, the store and the network layer). What differs is where the file lives, which account value enters its key, and the storage the game reads through. Steam's and GOG's saves share the local folder, and neither build reads the other's. The build number. Each build writes its build number at +0x14 of the decrypted file: 0x22AA (8874) on Steam and the Store, 0x98D (2445) on GOG. The GOG executable has 0x98D at the same three mov r8d sites and one cmp where Steam's has 0x22AA. The profile loader 0x17C6500 reads the value into a local and never compares it, so a save written by one build loads in another once it is encrypted with that build's account value (and, for the Store, its key constants). A profile that fails to load is not kept: any load status but 1 sends the loader to the new-profile reset 0x17C4D6C, which starts the introduction, and the game then saves that empty profile over the old file.

Where compared, it does: one animation file's 523 patched sites hold the same bytes in both. - Whether the GOG build calls the four Steamworks functions it imports, and what it does when they answer nothing. - Which code reads or writes the GOG image's 8-byte .SHARED section. - Whether StoreConfiguration.IsStoreWebAccountId throws on every Windows installation or only on some; a start where it succeeds would show whether the Store build then keeps its saves. - Why the Store build's start-up pools are larger (14,809 inventory item objects against 10,223): a different pool configuration compiled in, or a different allocation path.

t: The executable: sections, functions, vtables, libraries
x: The Steam build's ShadowOfWar.exe is a 64-bit image of 117,732,784 bytes (the GOG and Microsoft Store executables are laid out differently; see Game builds). It has no relocation table ( IMAGE FILE RELOCS STRIPPED , no DYNAMIC BASE ), so it always loads at 0x140000000 and every code and static address is the same in every run; only heap addresses move. Control Flow Guard is off (load configuration of 148 bytes, no guard flags), so the image carries no compiler-made list of address-taken functions.

The section names do not describe their contents. Executability comes from each section's characteristics, not from its name: Section RVA range Access Contents --- --- --- --- .arch 0x0001000 - 0x1D87C00 read, execute the engine's code (about 30 MB) .sdata 0x1D88000 - 0x1D91400 read, execute HavokScript's interpreter: three functions, the first (0x1D88000, 13,176 bytes) the one that raises the script VM's run-time errors; the GOG build names this section .interpr .xtext 0x1D92000 - 0x25AC000 read read-only data: the vtables , strings, the GameDB schema metadata .idata 0x25AC000 - 0x2AA5000 read, write the writable globals: singletons, managers, static objects, startup tables .pdata 0x2AA5000 - 0x2C85000 read the exception directory: 163,575 unwind entries .bss a 0x2C89000 - 0x729714D read, write, execute 70 MB of code (below) .text 0x7299000 - 0x7299014 read, write 20 bytes, not executable Several further small sections hold the import and export directories, resources and other data. .bss a holds engine methods that are reached only through vtables: of 2,134 vtables with recovered starts, 1,847 have at least one method there, and 12,832 of 71,422 vtable slots point into it. None of those methods is the target of a direct call (0 of 400 sampled; the static call graph has 4,371 call sources in the section and no call targets), so a function there with no callers is not evidence of a wrong address. The section also holds a large amount of code that is not part of the engine's call graph: inside it, only data references (vtable slots, pointer tables) identify engine functions, and jump targets do not.

The exception directory is not the list of functions: - Leaf functions have no entry. The x64 ABI requires an unwind entry only for a function that needs unwinding; a leaf (no stack frame, no non-volatile registers touched, no calls) may omit it. The engine's StringHash 0x423E70, with more than 2,000 callers, is one of them. - 16.1% of the entries are fragments : 26,293 of 163,575 carry UNW FLAG CHAININFO and end with their parent's entry (8,140 directly after the parent, 11,001 within 64 KB, 7,152 far away as cold blocks; 12,232 functions own fragments). A fragment is entered by a jump, not a call. - Jump tables sit inline in .arch right after their function (the MSVC form lea rB, [ ImageBase]; mov eJ, [rB + rI 4 + T]; add rJ, rB; jmp rJ ), so a linear disassembly turns their bytes into millions of false instructions. Decoding must follow control flow from known starts and never continue past a terminator. - Tails : 4,822 call-free blocks outside every entry that a function jumps to and back from belong to that function. The function list is therefore 243,839 functions . Of these, 137,282 have their own unwind entry; the rest are leaves found as call targets, callbacks whose address is only ever loaded ( lea ), and methods referenced from vtables and pointer tables. 99.1% of the leaves start the way real functions start (16-byte aligned, or after int3 / nop padding, or directly after another function's body), against 97.0% for functions with an unwind entry. The unwind data is complete enough to walk any thread's stack frame by frame from its registers, which is how the frame timings in Threads and the frame were measured. A return address found by scanning a stack is not proof of a live frame: locals keep return addresses of earlier, deeper calls.

In the writable globals, 33,354 qword slots are zero in the file and hold code pointers once the game has started (21,343 distinct targets): registration tables that startup code fills with lea rdx, [function] followed by a call to a register function (only 1,044 slots are written by a direct mov ). Across two launches the slots and their targets agreed with a Jaccard index of 0.9997 over 33,347 slots; the few differences are run-time state (a stored return address and a captured call stack), not tables.

The C runtime entry 0x8C3E5C runs initterm e(0x1DA8778, 0x1DA8798) (C initializers) and initterm(0x1D93950, 0x1DA8760) : 10,690 C++ global constructors , in link order. The first global each constructor writes increases along the table in 8,043 of 9,483 steps (84.8%): data is laid out per object file. Code is not: across 18,206 functions, the correlation between a function's address and the address of its private globals is 0.105 (Spearman), the signature of whole-program optimization reordering code. Only local runs survive (functions bracketed by one source file's strings belong to that file in 451 of 454 cases). Of the constructors, 649 register developer-console entries. Each is the same 0x7C-byte body: thread-safe initialization of the console registry, the static object 0x2A58BC0 (vt 0x1EC6488, a critical section and a sorted entry list, guard 0x2A58BB0, built by 0x816CF4), Register(entry) (registry slot 12), then atexit(unregister) . The registry's Execute is 0x15D0338, Find 0x7CBBA4 and Register 0x77F54C.

Vtables are read-only data in .xtext . 1,546 classes carry MSVC run-time type information (a complete-object locator before the vtable). About 4,100 more do not: 5,007 runs of two or more function pointers in .xtext are loaded by a lea and have no type information; for 4,097 of them (81.8%) the constructor pattern holds, the run's address being stored at [object+0] , against 1,399 of 1,746 (80.1%) for vtables with type information. CResourceBundle (0x1E6E678, 18 slots, constructors 0x3DB434 and 0x3DB6EC) is one of the classes without it. Vtables without type information pack back to back with no separator, so a table's end is the next table's start, and a start needs evidence: a code reference, a data pointer or a run-time pointer to it. A string-guessed start inside another table cuts that table short: the NPC class vt 0x1FB3640 has at least 129 slots (its per-frame AI update is slot 119, and slots 121, 122 and 128 are in use). Multiple inheritance shows as tables side by side: an inventory item's primary vtable 0x1FDABF8 has one slot and its secondary vtable, stored at +0x18 , is 0x1FDABD0 with five. The C runtime's initializer table is not a vtable even though it is a long run of code pointers in .xtext . Live census. Walking the allocators of a running game (Minas Ithil) and testing each allocation's first qword against every known vtable finds 2.51 million objects of 2,518 classes , about two thirds of them of classes without type information. The most instantiated class is vt 0x1DBC010 (176,706 objects at a stride of 0x38). Consecutive instances repeat at a fixed stride, which bounds the object's size from above: inventory items repeat every 0x118 bytes, a CResourceBundle (0x178 bytes) every 0x180 and an NPC (0x3180 bytes by its class descriptor) every 0x3188. A class's runtime implementation of a GameDB record type can be recognized from what its methods read. A class whose methods read fields of one category (at least three reads, at least 60% of them) implements that record type. This rule names 195 classes, 184 of them without type information, among them the AI planner steps (see AI).

The build uses link-time code generation, and it shows in the calling convention. Values stay in volatile registers across calls to functions the compiler proved do not touch them. Computing each function's written registers as a fixed point over the call graph shows that 61,578 of 133,050 callees preserve at least one volatile general-purpose register, and that between 74,179 and 83,251 preserve a given xmm register (0x1C0B634 keeps the screen width in xmm1 across the screen-height accessor). Analysis that assumes every call clobbers rax, rcx, rdx, r8-r11 loses these values. The linker also folds identical functions . Many script bindings share one implementation, so a function address claimed by many bindings is not an identity: the engine assert 0x819104 (3,226 call sites), the 5-byte operator delete thunk 0x8C4370 (4,839 callers) and the record-name getter 0x18BDB0 (2,203) each sit under many binding names. Binding stubs are packed back to back with no padding (a ret at 0x1B75A4B, the next stub's mov r11, rsp at 0x1B75A4C).

Identified from library strings and source paths, the namespaces of type information, imports, known constants (CRC32, FNV, SHA, MD5, AES tables) and contiguity (libraries link as contiguous object files; a gap bracketed by one library belongs to it, with 622 of 626 held-out anchors confirmed), 13,886 functions belong to linked libraries : Library Functions --- --- Havok (physics, AI navigation, cloth) 8,090 MSVC standard library 2,793 OpenSSL 1,897 Hydra (the publisher's online-services client) 619 Steamworks 327 HavokScript 61 Bink 45 Wwise 34 zlib 17 Exports. The executable exports 286 named symbols with their full C++ signatures. Of these, 263 belong to Wwise (the AK::SoundEngine API and its Query , MemoryMgr , StreamMgr , DynamicSequence , Monitor , MotionEngine , MusicEngine and DynamicDialogue namespaces, and globals such as g pRegistryMgr and g pRTPCMgr ; see Audio and video). The rest are Scaleform's system and matrix functions, two memory pool ids and an assert hook. With the run-time type information they are the binary's only exact symbol names. The GOG build exports the same names plus GetModuleVersion ; the Microsoft Store build exports no Wwise API and instead 284 functions of the C++ REST SDK (see Game builds). The online layer also links the Apache Avro C library ( avro record set , src\Core\avFloatType.cpp ). Small routines were identified by running them in an emulator against reference implementations: 13 functions behave as memcpy and 5 as strlen , plus CRC32, FNV-1a and the engine's string hash. A string-copy test needs inputs that a fixed-size copy cannot pass. The quaternion copy 0x7FE6EC (a fixed loop of four dwords) and the transform copy 0x7FD96C both return their destination and copy more than the 11 bytes in which a pair of test strings differ, so a test that compares only those bytes reports them as strcpy . StringHash 0x423E70 (the P919 name hash, h = h 919 + LUT[c] with the table at 0x1DB50D0) takes its seed in r8 and never clears its accumulator, so callers chain hashes; a caller that leaves a value in r8 gets a different hash.

The engine allocates through Doug Lea's malloc 2.8.x, built with mspaces, two copies linked in . One copy has its parameters at 0x277CDD8 and its global state at 0x277CE10; the other has its parameters at 0x277D1E8 ( create mspace 0x1176058, sys alloc 0x11744F8). Segments come from VirtualAlloc . In malloc state , +0x358 is the footprint, +0x370 the flags and +0x3A0 the segment list {base, size, next, flags} . A chunk head is size 1 previous-in-use 2 in-use, user memory starts at chunk + 16, and a 0xB fencepost closes each segment. In one running game a single state of the second copy owned 123 segments summing exactly to its 2,695 MB footprint , 78% of the process's heap memory: 1,086,315 chunks, 2,663 MB in use. The engine keeps a family of scaled clocks. Each is a holder object with its own vtable (vt 0x22F2E90 to vt 0x22F2F10), and the holder's +0x08 is the clock state (vt 0x22C2570): State offset Holds --- --- +0x08 the number of objects that use the clock as their time source +0x10 , +0x14 the current step, in milliseconds (u32) and in seconds (f32) +0x18 , +0x20 the time, in milliseconds (u32) and in seconds (f64) +0x28 / +0x2C the rate's numerator and denominator +0x30 the scale +0x34 the effective rate of the last step (f32) +0x38 , +0x3C the smallest and the largest step, in milliseconds +0x40 a stop byte +0x44 extra milliseconds, added once to the next step from +0x60 a list of listeners The update (vf2 0x59A2F50) computes the step as the rate times the real elapsed time, plus the pending extra, which it then clears. While the stop byte is set or the rate's denominator exceeds 0xFFFF, it forces the step to 0 and skips the clamp; otherwise it clamps the step to [+0x38, +0x3C] . It then passes the step to every listener's vf2. Six clocks clamp to 1-100 ms, so a long hitch advances them by at most 100 ms; the unscaled and real-time clocks have no upper bound ( +0x3C = 0xFFFFFFFF). The clock slots form a run of 11 from 0x2702548 to 0x2702598. Eight have a known role, and three more fill the gaps between them: Clock Slot --- --- world [base+0x2702598] player [base+0x2702548] combat companion [base+0x2702570] world UI [base+0x2702558] presentations [base+0x2702578] an unscaled clock [base+0x2702550] UI [base+0x2702588] a real-time clock [base+0x2702590] unnamed; one ClientFX manager outside the client shell runs on it [base+0x2702560] unnamed [base+0x2702568] unnamed [base+0x2702580] Every clock but the real-time one stops while the game is paused. In a paused game the seven pausable clocks read stop byte 1 and step 0 and did not advance at all, while the real-time clock read stop byte 0, steps of 3-4 ms and a rate of 1.0, and advanced 1,015 ms in one second. Slow motion scales the first five clocks in the table as channels (see Quests, story and scenes). The count at +0x08 is a reference count that includes the clock's own holder: the presentations clock reads 1, and its only reference is the holder's +0x08 . On each of the 11 live clock states the heap holds exactly two more pointers to the state than +0x08 says, and those two are the state's own +0x58 and +0x80 , which point back at it. So the world clock's count, 113,151 in a loaded Lithlad, is 113,150 users and the holder, against 31 on the player clock and 477 on the UI clock in the same scene. A ClientFX manager takes two references to its clock. A character's time source [char+0x88] is the state of one of these clocks: 114 of 115 characters in the spawn manager use the world clock and the player uses the player clock. The object update scheduler subtracts that clock's step from each object's countdown (see Threads and the frame), so pausing (step 0.0) and slow motion throttle NPC and player updates through the same values. AI services run on the world time instead: each service is due when the world time at +0x20 passes its own due time.

- The spawn manager [base+0x26FFBE8] is null at the main menu and live once a world is loaded. The player object persists across menus, so its presence proves nothing. A world is in play when the spawn manager exists and holds spawned characters. - Spawn manager layout. +0x190 is the number of characters owned by ambient spawning, not the length of the character array. Entries are 0x40 bytes with the character at +0x20 . The manager is reallocated during travel, so a pointer to it must be re-read on every use; the same holds for character controllers, which are replaced on respawn. - A load starting shows as a new pointer at [CGameClientShell]+0xE50 . - Pause. The simulation pauses while the game window is unfocused: the world time stops and the per-object time steps are 0, while the renderer keeps drawing at full rate. - Loads rebuild state. Some loading screens deserialize GameDB instance data and faction members again, and a region change resets bundles and animation state, so values written into those objects before a load do not survive it.

Anything that allocates engine objects, dispatches to scripts or rebuilds a world object runs on the main thread; the render thread consumes commands the main thread posts (see Threads and the frame). Engine asserts are a write to a null address at 0x819113 with the message in rcx ( EngineAssert 0x819104).
